newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Oil majors in pact to consider merging gas fields.
newsitem.headline: Oil majors in pact to consider merging gas fields.

text.p: Major international oil companies were on Tuesday said to be close to an agreement that could lead to two of Australia's biggest offshore gas fields being developed jointly at one massive processing plant.

Mobil Corp, part owner of the big Gorgon field off northwest Australia, said it expected the Gorgon joint venturers to sign an agreement by the end of June to look at merging the field's development with the giant North West Shelf project.
Mobil's Australian unit, Mobil Australia, said three of the four Gorgon joint venturers had signed a "cooperative development" protocol, including Mobil.
The Gorgon partners are Mobil, with a one-seventh stake, and Texaco, Chevron Inc and Royal Dutch/Shell Group, each with a two-sevenths stake.
"We are hopeful that (a protocol) will happen before the end of the month," Mobil Australia's general manager of corporate affairs, David Byers, told Reuters.

"There's been a protocol which has been developed...it's between the four partners. Three have signed off on the protocol, and we are one of them, and I obviously can't say who the fourth party is (that has not signed)."

"The fourth party is still looking at the details," Byers added. "You would expect there will still be a bit of going back and forth on the details, but we are hopeful of having everything signed off on the protocol by the end of this month."
Gorgon, one of Australia's biggest gas fields, lies near the North West Shelf project.

The North West Shelf partners are The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, British Petroleum Co, Japan Australia LNG (MiMi) Pty Ltd, which is a partnership of Mitsui and Co Ltd and Mitsubishi Corp, Chevron, Royal Dutch/Shell and Woodside Petroleum Ltd.
The North West Shelf project's liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant on the Burrup Peninsula of Western Australia has a capacity of 7.5 million tonnes per annum (MTPA).
The partners propose to double capacity at a cost of A$5 billion (US$3.8 billion), based on long-term demand from Japan.
Gorgon has capacity to produce six MTPA of LNG.

Gorgon partners Mobil and Texaco have been examining the feasibility of a stand-alone LNG plant to bring the field on stream, but the idea of expanding the existing North West Shelf plant further to process the Gorgon gas is gaining momentum.

This would mean expanding the Burrup Peninsula plant from its existing four production trains to seven, including two extra trains now proposed by the North West Shelf partners and another two to cater for the Gorgon gas.
Each new train can produce three to four MTPA, implying a massive LNG plant producing about 21 MTPA, if the existing expansion proposal proceeds and Gorgon is folded in.
The North West Shelf operator, Woodside, on Tuesday said the protocol talks were limited to the Gorgon partners.
A Woodside spokesman told Reuters the North West Shelf partners were open to any proposals to bring Gorgon into the project, but no formal proposal had been received.

The protocol will canvass ways of merging the development of the two fields, and will be followed by a study to assess the best option, Byers said. The protocol itself would not amount to a go-ahead for cooperative development, he added.
The Gorgon partners will then compare the feasibility of a greenfields plant with a cooperative development, he said.
The only Gorgon partner yet to sign the protocol has not done so due to matters of detail, Byers said.
"They are not areas of significance," he added.
